citation: Sakai JT, Chintaluru Y, Raymond KM, McWilliams S, Carter RM, Winters DE, Mikulich-Gilbertson SK (2023). A revised prosocial behavior game: testing associations with psychopathic traits and the effects of moral elevation using a randomized clinical trial. PLOS ONE 18(4):e0283279
arm_label: Moral elevation video (subway rescue) vs control nature video
country: USA (inferred, not stated in the paper: online sample recruited via Craigslist; authors and IRB are in Colorado; payment in $)
treatment_description: Moral elevation video depicting a man risking his life to save another in the New York subway, shown between Run 1 and Run 2 of the game.
control_description: Nature video of similar length (series of images of the ocean, green spaces and forests).
outcome_description: AlAn's Short Game v.2, Run 2 vs Run 1: number of prosocial decisions (Active Type A trials rejected, where self gains and Red Cross loses, plus Active Type B trials accepted, where self loses and Red Cross gains).
quote: The Group by Run interaction was non-significant (F1, 478 = 2.40; p = 0.122)
location: Results, 'Testing the effects of moral elevation on game behavior' (same F also in the Fig 4 caption, given there as p = 0.12); group ns from Fig 4 caption
notes: F is the Group x Run interaction from a mixed-model ANCOVA (random subject effect, unstructured covariance; fixed effects Group, Run and sex; covariates age, race and Red Cross visual analog scale; sex interactions non-significant and removed), i.e. the between-group difference in pre- to post-video change. Group main effect F(1,478) = 0.42, p = 0.52; Run main effect F(1,478) = 2.25, p = 0.13. DIRECTION: values.sign = null. No text, table or caption states which group changed more or in which direction. The paper says only 'both Groups (control and moral elevation video) showed relatively stable levels of prosocial behavior across runs 1 and 2' (Results), 'we did not find that moral elevation stimulus exposure led to changes in prosocial behavior' (Discussion), and refers to 'the lack of change in prosocial behavior in the control group'. Fig 4 plots adjusted estimates with SE but its caption gives no numbers; the verifier could not open the figure image. No means or SDs by group and run are reported in the text or tables. EFFECT-SIZE CAUTION: an F for a Group x Run interaction converted with n_t and n_c gives a standardized difference in change scores; the authors report Run 1 and Run 2 as highly correlated (high test-retest reliability), so this is not on the same scale as a post-test between-group d. SAMPLE: 500 recruited (250 per group planned); analysed modified ITT n = 485 (randomized plus completed baseline). Methods call the elevation arm Group 1, Results call the control arm Group 1; the Fig 4 caption names the arms by video (elevation n = 237, control n = 248), so the ns are unambiguous. Ages 18 to 25; protocol completed online via REDCap; within-sex permuted-blocks randomization scheme created by the study statistician. The sample's country and state are not stated. INCENTIVES: 'Subjects were paid $20 plus earnings from playing the AlAn's Short Game v.2' (Methods), so own payoffs were real and each prosocial choice cost the subject money. The game starts with $2.50 for the subject and a $2.50 Red Cross donation; the paper never says the Red Cross allocation was actually donated, nor that it was hypothetical. Players are told no information on how they played will be shared with others. No manipulation check ('we did not measure self-reported moral elevation'). TREATMENT: the paper says only that the video 'depicts a man risking his life to save another in the New York subway' and 'has been used in prior moral elevation studies'; it does not say whether it is news footage of a real event, and gives no length for either video. Coded modern_invented as the nearest category. Target coded stranger (charity recipient). No outcome is labelled primary in the paper; this is the only test of the elevation main effect (the paper also tests moderation of the psychopathy association: Group x Factor 1 x Run F(1,474) = 0.10, p = 0.76). REGISTRATION: the paper states 'the study protocol was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03834467)'; it gives no enrollment dates and does not say whether registration was prospective. The verifier could not open the registry record, so registration timing and the registered primary outcome are unverified.
verifier_changes: values: added sign = null; no text, table or figure caption states which group changed more or in which direction, and the Fig 4 image could not be opened
country: changed 'USA (Colorado; online via Craigslist)' to mark the country as inferred; the paper does not state the sample's country or state (Colorado is where the authors and IRB are)
quote: removed the trailing period; in the paper the sentence goes on: 'indicating that there was no significant difference in change in prosocial behavior between Groups'
location: added that the same F appears in the Fig 4 caption, where p is given as 0.12
notes: removed the claim that the treatment is a 'real-event video'; the paper does not say so, only that it depicts the subway rescue and 'has been used in prior moral elevation studies'
notes: added sex as a fixed effect in the model (A listed only age, race and Red Cross VAS) and the Run main effect F(1,478) = 2.25, p = 0.13

notes: added the direction evidence, the effect-size scale caution (change-score metric), the exact incentive wording, the absence of a manipulation check, the age range, and the unverified registration timing

citation: Lombardi E, Valle A, Rinaldi T, Massaro D, Marchetti A (2021). Learning to wait and be altruistic: testing a conversational training in economic education for primary school children. Europe's Journal of Psychology 17(4):306-318. doi:10.5964/ejop.2453
country: Italy (two schools, Northern Italy near Milan)
treatment_description: Conversational training in economic education: 'three one-hour sessions each, conducted in class by a researcher' (p. 310) over 'about two weeks of school time', starting one week after pre-test; topics fairness, altruism and delay of gratification; two stories per topic, 'invented or created based on children's (Varela, 2014 [Fair is fair]) or on scientific literature (Larsen et al., 2017)'; each story followed by four multiple-choice questions (comprehension, perspective-taking) and group discussion. Abstract: stories 'relaying values of fairness, altruism, and delayed gratification' (p. 306)
control_description: Business-as-usual: 'Children in the CG only attended civics education classes, established in their state curricula' (p. 308); 'regular school program of citizenship education' (p. 307). No-text control (flag per protocol); authors list the lack of a matched neutral-content training as a limitation (p. 313)
delay: delayed: post-test one week after the end of the three training sessions
outcome_description: Dictator game (Kahneman et al., 1986): child as Dictator decides how to distribute 10 trading cards 'between him and a passive player'; 'the other child (the Receiver) was presented as a drawing image' (p. 309), called 'a schoolmate depicted in a drawing' in the Discussion (p. 311); one round, offered number of cards scored (0-10 implied by 10 cards, range not printed for DG); real cards
quote: children in the TG showed significantly higher post-test offers compared to the post-test offers in the CG, F(1, 108) = 5.431, p = .022
notes: F is from 'Pairwise comparisons' of post-test offers ('as shown in Figure 1') within the repeated-measures GLM with covariate; printed eta2 = .071, theta = 0.700 (theta undefined). Sign 1: the paper states TG post-test offers were higher than CG post-test offers (p. 310); Abstract: TG 'showed significant improvement at the post-test in altruistic and investment behaviour' (p. 306). Receiver: Method says only 'the other child (the Receiver) was presented as a drawing image' (p. 309); the Discussion describes the receiver as another hypothetical but well defined child, 'a schoolmate depicted in a drawing' (p. 311), so target coded ingroup (anonymous schoolmate). The paper does not say whether any real receiver got the cards; the giving was costly to the child. Assignment by class: 'Two classes for each age range participated and for every range one class was randomly assigned to the CG' (p. 307), i.e. cluster randomization of 6 classes (3 per arm) in two schools near Milan; analysis is at child level and does not model clustering. N recruited 121; excluded 6 TG and 3 CG for incomplete pre/post sessions and 2 CG with under 3 months in Italy; final N = 110 aged 8-10 (TG n = 55, CG n = 55) (p. 307). Pre-test, training one week later, post-test 'one week after training sessions end'; post-test phase ended about 4 months after pre-test (p. 308). Analysis: GLM for repeated measures, time within, group between, verbal ability as covariate (groups differed at pre-test only on verbal ability, t(108) = 2,376 as printed, p = .019; other variables 'didn't show any statistically significant differences', p. 310). 'Decision making tasks were played for real, giving a final amount of trading cards' (p. 308). No outcome is designated primary. Treatment mixes stories with questions and discussion and also targets delay of gratification. Story texts are in supplementary Appendix 1 (PsychArchives, doi:10.23668/psycharchives.5242); the article says only that the stories relay values of fairness and altruism, adapted from Varela (2014) 'Fair is fair' and Larsen et al. (2017) prosocial storybooks. No means or SDs for any decision task in the main text; Figure 1 (p. 311) plots DG proposals by group at pre and post (image not read); descriptives are in Appendix 2, which could not be opened (the WebFetch permission request for the PsychArchives page timed out). Results have no subheadings. No group x time interaction statistic is reported. Reporting inconsistencies: with a covariate the error df should be 107, but 108 is printed; the printed eta2 values for DG (.071) and DT (.006) do not match their F(1, 108) (implied partial eta2 about .048 and .001), whereas the Investment Task's F = 4.270 and eta2 = .038 agree, so the F and eta2 for DG and DT may come from different tests. Ultimatum Game: children were Responders only, tested with within-group McNemar tests; not a P outcome, not recorded. Preregistration not mentioned. Funded by Feduf via Fondazione Nord Milano; no competing interests.

notes: added the 'Pairwise comparisons' wording, printed theta = 0.700, the Abstract evidence for sign 1, and that the paper does not say whether a real receiver got the cards.

treatment_description: 'stories (invented or from Varela 2014 / Larsen et al. 2017)' corrected to the paper's wording 'invented or created based on' those sources; added 'over about two weeks', the start one week after pre-test, the question content and the Abstract quote on story values; kept the paper's ambiguous 'three one-hour sessions each'.
control_description: added 'regular school program of citizenship education' (p. 307), business-as-usual label and the authors' own limitation note (p. 313).
location: '(Results, Dictator Game)' / '(Results, Donation Task)' changed to '(Results; no subheadings)'; the Results section has no subheadings. Page 310 confirmed.
notes: location of the randomization quote corrected from p. 308 to p. 307.
notes: location of 'Decision making tasks were played for real' corrected from p. 309 to p. 308.

notes: 'Means/SDs appear only in Figure 1 (DG, values not printed)' replaced; the main text has no means/SDs for any decision task, Figure 1 plots DG by group (image not read), Appendix 2 not reachable (WebFetch permission request timed out).

notes: added exclusion counts (121 recruited, 11 excluded), clustering not modelled, story-content evidence, and the reporting inconsistencies (df 108 printed where 107 expected with a covariate; eta2 for DG and DT inconsistent with their F, Investment Task consistent).
notes: added funding and competing-interest statements.
